chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: Pierre knew this large room well—divided by columns and an arch, its walls hung with Persian carpets. The area behind the columns, with a tall silk-curtained mahogany bed on one side and an enormous icon case on the other, was bathed in red light like a Russian church during evening services. Beneath the gleaming icons stood a long reclining chair, and in it, propped on smooth white pillows that had obviously just been changed, Pierre saw the familiar, majestic figure of his father, Count Bezukhov—covered to the waist by a bright green quilt, with that gray mane of hair above his broad forehead that always made one think of a lion, and the deep, noble wrinkles of his handsome, ruddy face. He lay directly beneath the icons, his large, thick hands resting on top of the quilt. A wax taper had been placed between the forefinger and thumb of his right hand, which lay palm-down, and an old servant standing behind the chair held it in place. By the chair stood the priests, their long hair falling over magnificent, glittering vestments, holding lighted tapers and slowly, solemnly conducting the service. A little behind them stood the two younger princesses, holding handkerchiefs to their eyes. In front of them their eldest sister, Catiche, stood with a fierce and resolute expression fixed on the icons, as if declaring to everyone that she could not be held responsible for what might happen if she looked away. Anna Mikhaylovna stood by the door with a meek, sorrowful, all-forgiving expression, near the unfamiliar lady. Prince Vasili stood at the front, near the reclining chair, a wax taper in his left hand, his left arm resting on the carved back of a velvet chair he had turned around for the purpose, crossing himself with his right hand and raising his eyes heavenward each time his fingers touched his forehead. His face wore a look of calm piety and submission to God's will. "If you don't understand these feelings," his expression seemed to say, "so much the worse for you."

Behind him stood the aide-de-camp, the doctors, and the manservants. The men and women had separated as in a church. Everyone crossed themselves silently, and the only sounds were the reading of the service, the muffled chanting of deep bass voices, and in the pauses, sighs and the shuffling of feet. Anna Mikhaylovna, with an air of importance showing she knew exactly what she was doing, crossed the room to Pierre and handed him a taper. He lit it and, distracted by watching those around him, began crossing himself with the hand that held the candle.

Sophie, the rosy, youngest princess with the mole—the one who was always laughing—watched him. She smiled, buried her face in her handkerchief, and kept it hidden for a moment. Then she looked up, saw Pierre again, and couldn't help laughing once more. She clearly couldn't look at him without laughing, yet couldn't resist looking. To remove herself from temptation, she slipped quietly behind one of the columns. In the middle of the service, the priests' voices suddenly stopped. They whispered to each other, and the old servant holding the count's hand stood up and said something to the ladies. Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward and, bending over the dying man, beckoned to Lorrain from behind her back. The French doctor had no taper; he was leaning against one of the columns in a respectful posture that showed he—a foreigner—despite all differences of faith, fully understood the significance of the rite being performed and even approved of it. He now approached the sick man with the noiseless step of a person in full health, lifted the hand that lay free from the green quilt with his delicate white fingers, turned slightly to one side, and felt the pulse, reflecting for a moment. The sick man was given something to drink. There was a brief commotion around him, then everyone returned to their places and the service continued. During this pause, Pierre noticed that Prince Vasili left the chair he had been leaning on and—with an air suggesting that he knew what he was doing, and if others didn't understand, that was their problem—walked past the dying man without stopping, joined the eldest princess, and moved with her to the side of the room where the tall bed stood with its silk hangings. They both slipped out through a back door, then returned to their places one after the other before the service concluded. Pierre paid no more attention to this than to anything else going on around him, having decided once and for all that whatever was happening that evening was somehow essential.

The chanting stopped, and the priest's voice was heard respectfully congratulating the dying man on having received the sacrament. The dying man lay as lifeless and motionless as before. People began to stir around him—footsteps, whispers—among which Anna Mikhaylovna's voice was the most audible.
Pierre heard her say:
"He really must be moved to the bed. It's impossible here..."

The sick man was so surrounded by doctors, princesses, and servants that Pierre could no longer see the ruddy, yellowish face with its gray mane—though he hadn't lost sight of it for a single moment during the entire service, even while watching other faces. He could tell from the careful movements of those crowded around the reclining chair that they were lifting the dying man and carrying him.

"Hold onto my arm or you'll drop him!" one of the servants said in a frightened whisper. "Get a grip from underneath. Here!" voices called out, and the heavy breathing of the bearers and the scraping of their feet grew more urgent, as though the weight they carried was too much for them.

As the bearers—among them Anna Mikhaylovna—passed the young man, he caught a momentary glimpse between their heads and shoulders of the dying man's broad, uncovered chest and powerful shoulders, raised by those gripping him under the arms, and of his gray, curly, lion-like head. That head, with its remarkably wide brow and cheekbones, its handsome, sensual mouth, and its cold, majestic expression, was not disfigured by the approach of death. It looked just as Pierre remembered it from three months earlier, when the count had sent him to Petersburg. But now the head swayed helplessly with the uneven movements of the bearers, and those cold, indifferent eyes were fixed on nothing.

After a few minutes of commotion around the tall bed, the bearers dispersed. Anna Mikhaylovna touched Pierre's hand and said, "Come." Pierre went with her to the bed where the sick man had been laid in a stately pose befitting the ceremony just completed. He lay with his head propped high on the pillows, his hands placed symmetrically on the green silk quilt, palms down. When Pierre approached, the count was gazing straight at him—but with an expression whose meaning no living person could decipher. Either the look meant nothing at all, just that eyes must look somewhere as long as they exist, or it meant far too much. Pierre hesitated, unsure what to do, and glanced at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna made a quick gesture with her eyes toward the sick man's hand, moving her lips as if sending it a kiss. Pierre carefully craned his neck, trying not to touch the quilt, and pressed his lips to the large, fleshy hand with its heavy bones. Neither the hand nor a single muscle of the count's face moved. Pierre looked again at Anna Mikhaylovna, asking what to do next. She indicated a chair beside the bed with her eyes. Pierre sat down obediently, his expression silently asking whether he was doing the right thing. Anna Mikhaylovna nodded her approval. Once again Pierre assumed the naively symmetrical pose of an Egyptian statue, clearly distressed that his large, clumsy body took up so much space, doing his best to appear as small as possible. He looked at the count, who still stared at the spot where Pierre's face had been before he sat down. Anna Mikhaylovna's manner conveyed her awareness of the solemn importance of these final moments between father and son. This lasted about two minutes, though to Pierre it felt like an hour. Suddenly the broad muscles of the count's face began to twitch. The twitching grew stronger, the handsome mouth was pulled to one side—and only now did Pierre grasp how close his father was to death—and from that distorted mouth came a faint, hoarse sound. Anna Mikhaylovna watched the sick man's eyes intently, trying to read what he wanted. She pointed first to Pierre, then to a drink, then whispered Prince Vasili's name inquiringly, then pointed to the quilt. The dying man's eyes and face showed impatience. He made an effort to look at the servant who stood at the head of the bed.
"He wants to be turned onto his other side," the servant whispered, and rose to turn the count's heavy body toward the wall.
Pierre got up to help.

As the count was being turned, one of his arms fell back limply, and he made a futile effort to pull it forward. Whether he noticed the look of horror with which Pierre stared at that lifeless arm, or whether some other thought crossed his dying mind, he glanced at the disobedient arm, then at Pierre's terrified face, then back at the arm, and a faint, pitiful smile appeared on his face—completely at odds with his features—as though mocking his own helplessness. At the sight of that smile, Pierre felt an unexpected tremor in his chest and a prickling in his nose, and tears blurred his eyes. The sick man was turned onto his side, facing the wall. He sighed.
"He's dozing," said Anna Mikhaylovna, noticing one of the princesses coming to take her turn at the bedside watch. "Let's go."
Pierre went out.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: By now, no one remained in the reception room except Prince Vasili and the eldest princess, who sat beneath the portrait of Catherine the Great, talking urgently. The moment they saw Pierre and his companion, they fell silent. Pierre thought he caught the princess hiding something as she whispered:
"I can't stand the sight of that woman."
"Catiche has had tea set up in the small drawing room," Prince Vasili told Anna Mikhaylovna. "Go and have something, my poor Anna Mikhaylovna, or you won't hold up."
To Pierre he said nothing, only gave his arm a sympathetic squeeze below the shoulder. Pierre followed Anna Mikhaylovna into the small drawing room.

"There is nothing quite so refreshing after a sleepless night as a cup of this delicious Russian tea," Lorrain was saying with restrained animation, standing and sipping from a delicate Chinese handleless cup before a table set with tea things and a cold supper in the small circular room. Everyone who was at Count Bezukhov's house that night had gathered here to fortify themselves. Pierre remembered this circular drawing room with its mirrors and small tables well. During balls at the house, Pierre—who didn't know how to dance—used to like sitting here, watching the ladies pass through in their ball gowns with diamonds and pearls on bare shoulders, admiring themselves in the brilliantly lit mirrors that multiplied their reflections. Now the same room was dimly lit by only two candles. On a small table, the tea things and supper dishes stood in disarray, and in the middle of the night a mixed group of people sat there—not celebrating but whispering somberly, every word and gesture showing that none of them could forget what was happening, and was about to happen, in the bedroom. Pierre ate nothing, though he very much wanted to. He looked inquiringly at his guide and saw that she was once again tiptoeing toward the reception room where they had left Prince Vasili and the eldest princess. Pierre decided this too must be essential, and after a short pause, followed her. Anna Mikhaylovna was standing beside the princess, and the two women were speaking in agitated whispers.
"Let me be the judge, Princess, of what is necessary and what is not," said the younger of the two, clearly in the same state of agitation as when she had slammed her door.

"But my dear princess," Anna Mikhaylovna answered calmly but firmly, positioning herself to block the way to the bedroom and prevent the other woman from passing, "won't this be too much for poor Uncle at a moment when he needs rest? Worldly matters at a time when his soul is already prepared..."

Prince Vasili sat in an armchair in his usual pose, one leg crossed high over the other. His flabby cheeks—which looked heavier at the bottom—were twitching violently, but he wore the air of a man unconcerned with what the two ladies were saying.
"Come now, my dear Anna Mikhaylovna, let Catiche do as she wishes. You know how fond the count is of her."

"I don't even know what's in this document," said the younger woman, turning to Prince Vasili and pointing at the inlaid portfolio in her hand. "All I know is that his real will is in his writing desk, and this is just a paper he's forgotten about...."
She tried to get past Anna Mikhaylovna, but Anna Mikhaylovna sprang forward to block her path.

"I know, my dear, kind princess," Anna Mikhaylovna said (in French), gripping the portfolio so tightly it was obvious she would not let go easily. "Dear princess, I beg you, I implore you—have some pity on him! I beseech you..."

The princess said nothing. The only sounds were their struggle over the portfolio. But it was clear that if the princess did speak, her words would not be kind to Anna Mikhaylovna. Despite her tenacious grip, Anna Mikhaylovna's voice lost none of its honeyed firmness and softness.
"Pierre, my dear, come here. I think he won't be out of place in a family discussion—don't you agree, Prince?"

"Why don't you speak, cousin?" the princess suddenly shrieked, so loudly that the people in the drawing room heard and were startled. "Why are you standing there in silence while heaven knows who takes it upon herself to interfere—making a scene on the very threshold of a dying man's room? You schemer!" she hissed viciously, and yanked the portfolio with all her might.
But Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward to maintain her grip and adjusted her hold.
Prince Vasili rose from his chair. "Oh!" he said with reproach and surprise. "This is absurd! Come, let go, I tell you."
The princess released her grip.
"And you too!"
But Anna Mikhaylovna did not obey.
"Let go, I tell you! I'll take responsibility. I'll go in and ask him myself. I!... Is that good enough for you?"

"But, Prince," said Anna Mikhaylovna, "after such a solemn sacrament, give him a moment's peace! Here, Pierre, tell them what you think," she said, turning to the young man, who had come close and was staring in astonishment at the princess's furious face—stripped of all dignity—and at Prince Vasili's twitching cheeks.
"Remember, you will answer for the consequences," Prince Vasili said severely. "You don't know what you're doing."
"Vile woman!" the princess shouted, lunging unexpectedly at Anna Mikhaylovna and snatching the portfolio from her hands.
Prince Vasili bowed his head and spread his hands in a helpless gesture.

At that moment, the terrible door—which Pierre had watched for so long, and which had always opened so quietly—burst open with a bang against the wall, and the second of the three sisters rushed out, wringing her hands.
"What are you doing!" she cried desperately. "He's dying, and you leave me alone with him!"

The eldest sister dropped the portfolio. Anna Mikhaylovna swooped down, snatched up the contested object, and ran into the bedroom. The eldest princess and Prince Vasili, recovering their composure, hurried after her. A few minutes later, the eldest sister emerged with a pale, rigid face, biting her lower lip again. When she caught sight of Pierre, her expression showed undisguised hatred.
"Yes, now you can celebrate!" she said. "This is what you've been waiting for." Then she burst into tears, covered her face with her handkerchief, and rushed from the room.

Prince Vasili came out next. He staggered to the sofa where Pierre was sitting and collapsed onto it, covering his face with his hand. Pierre noticed he was pale, and that his jaw was trembling and shaking as though he had a fever.

"Oh, my friend!" he said, gripping Pierre by the elbow. There was a sincerity and vulnerability in his voice that Pierre had never heard before. "How often we sin, how much we deceive—and for what? I'm nearly sixty, my dear friend... I too... It all ends in death. Death is terrible..." And he burst into tears.
Anna Mikhaylovna was the last to come out. She approached Pierre with slow, quiet steps.
"Pierre!" she said.
Pierre looked at her questioningly. She leaned forward and kissed the young man on his forehead, wetting him with her tears. After a pause, she said:
"He is gone...."
Pierre stared at her over his spectacles.
"Come, I'll go with you. Try to cry—nothing brings such relief as tears."

She led him into the dark drawing room, and Pierre was grateful that no one could see his face. Anna Mikhaylovna left him there, and when she returned, he had fallen asleep with his head resting on his arm.
The next morning, Anna Mikhaylovna said to Pierre:

"Yes, my dear, this is a great loss for all of us—to say nothing of you. But God will sustain you. You are young, and now, I hope, the master of an immense fortune. The will hasn't been opened yet. I know you well enough to be certain this won't go to your head, but it does impose responsibilities on you, and you must be a man."
Pierre said nothing.

"Perhaps I'll tell you someday, my dear boy, that if I hadn't been there, God only knows what would have happened. You know, your uncle promised me just the day before yesterday not to forget Boris. But he didn't have time. I hope, my dear friend, that you'll carry out your father's wishes?"

Pierre understood none of this and, blushing with embarrassment, looked at Princess Anna Mikhaylovna in silence. After her conversation with Pierre, Anna Mikhaylovna returned to the Rostovs' and went to bed. When she woke up the next morning, she told the Rostovs and all her acquaintances the details of Count Bezukhov's death. She said the count had died just as she herself would wish to die—that his end was not only moving but spiritually uplifting. As for the final meeting between father and son, it was so touching she could hardly think of it without tears, and she couldn't say who had shown more grace in those terrible moments—the father, who had remembered everyone at the last and spoken such tender words to his son, or Pierre, whose grief was heartbreaking to witness, though he had tried so hard to hide it to spare his dying father. "It's painful, but it does the soul good. It elevates you to see men like the old count and his worthy son," she said. About the eldest princess and Prince Vasili, she spoke disapprovingly—but only in whispers, and as a great secret.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: At Bald Hills, the estate of Prince Nicholas Andreevich Bolkonski, the arrival of young Prince Andrew and his wife was expected any day, but this didn't disrupt the old prince's rigid household routine. General-in-Chief Prince Nicholas Andreevich—nicknamed "the King of Prussia" in society—had been living at his country estate continuously since Emperor Paul had exiled him there, together with his daughter, Princess Mary, and her companion, Mademoiselle Bourienne. Though the new reign had made him free to return to the capitals, he continued to live in the country, remarking that anyone who wanted to see him could make the hundred-mile trip from Moscow to Bald Hills, while he himself needed nobody and nothing. He liked to say there are only two sources of human vice—idleness and superstition—and only two virtues—activity and intelligence. He personally oversaw his daughter's education, and to develop these two virtues in her, gave her lessons in algebra and geometry until she was twenty and organized her life so that every hour was accounted for. He himself was perpetually busy: writing his memoirs, solving problems in higher mathematics, turning snuffboxes on a lathe, working in the garden, or supervising the construction that was always underway on his estate. Since regularity is the first condition of productivity, regularity in his household was maintained to the highest degree of precision. He always came to meals not just at the same hour but at the same minute. With everyone around him, from his daughter down to the servants, the prince was sharp and unfailingly demanding—not out of cruelty, but with a severity that inspired the kind of fear and respect that few genuinely cruel men could have commanded. Although he was retired and no longer wielded political influence, every senior official appointed to the province felt duty-bound to pay him a visit, and they waited in his lofty antechamber—alongside the architect, the gardener, and Princess Mary—until the prince appeared at precisely the appointed time. Everyone in that waiting room experienced the same mix of respect and dread when the enormously tall study door swung open to reveal the small figure of the old man: powdered wig, small withered hands, and bushy gray eyebrows that, when he frowned, could hide the sharp gleam of his youthful, piercing eyes.

On the morning of the day the young couple was expected, Princess Mary entered the antechamber at the usual time for the morning greeting, crossing herself nervously and repeating a silent prayer. She came in like this every morning, and every morning she prayed the encounter would go smoothly.
An old powdered manservant sitting in the antechamber stood quietly and said in a whisper: "Please go in."

Through the door came the steady hum of a lathe. The princess timidly pushed open the door, which moved silently on its hinges. She paused at the threshold. The prince was working at the lathe and, after a quick glance, went on with what he was doing.

The enormous study was full of objects clearly in constant use. A large table strewn with books and plans, tall glass-fronted bookcases with keys in their locks, a high standing desk with an open exercise book on it, the lathe with tools at the ready and shavings scattered around—everything spoke of continuous, varied, disciplined activity. The rhythmic motion of his small foot in a silver-embroidered Tartar boot, and the firm pressure of his lean, sinewy hand, showed that the prince still possessed all the endurance and energy of a hardy old age. After a few more turns of the lathe, he removed his foot from the pedal, wiped his chisel, dropped it into a leather pouch attached to the lathe, and walked to the table to greet his daughter. He never gave his children a blessing, so he simply offered his bristly, unshaven cheek and, looking at her with tender attention, said sternly:
"Feeling well? Good. Sit down." He took the exercise book of geometry lessons he had written himself and pulled up a chair with his foot.
"For tomorrow!" he said, quickly finding the right page and marking a section with a hard fingernail, scratching from one paragraph to the next.
The princess bent over the exercise book on the table.
"Wait—here's a letter for you," the old man said suddenly, pulling a letter in a woman's handwriting from a bag hanging above the table and tossing it to her.
Red blotches appeared on the princess's face at the sight of the letter. She snatched it up quickly and bent her head over it.
"From Heloise?" the prince asked with a cold smile that revealed his still-sound, yellowish teeth.
"Yes, it's from Julie," the princess replied with a timid glance and a shy smile.
"I'll let two more letters pass, but the third one I'm reading," the prince said sternly. "I'm afraid you write a lot of nonsense. I'll read the third!"
"Read this one if you like, Father," said the princess, blushing even more and holding out the letter.
"The third, I said the third!" the prince snapped, pushing the letter away. He leaned his elbows on the table and drew the geometry exercise book toward him.

"Now then, young lady," he began, bending over the book close to his daughter and resting his arm on the back of her chair, so that she found herself enveloped on all sides by the sharp scent of old age and tobacco that she had known all her life. "Now then—these triangles are equal. Please observe that the angle ABC..."

The princess stared with frightened eyes at her father's face, which glittered with intensity right next to hers. The red patches came and went on her cheeks, and it was obvious she understood nothing and was so terrified that her fear would block any comprehension of his explanations, no matter how clear. Whether the fault lay with the teacher or the student, the same thing happened every day: the princess's eyes glazed over, she could neither see nor hear, conscious only of her stern father's withered face close to hers, his breath and his smell, able to think of nothing but escaping to her own room to work out the problem in peace. The old man would lose his composure, noisily shoving his chair back and forth, struggling to hold his temper—and nearly always failing. He would scold her, and sometimes hurl the exercise book across the room.
The princess gave a wrong answer.
"Now, isn't she a fool!" the prince shouted, shoving the book aside and turning sharply away. But he immediately stood up, paced the room, gently touched his daughter's hair, and sat down again.
He pulled his chair closer and resumed his explanation.

"This won't do, Princess, it won't do," he said as Princess Mary closed the exercise book with tomorrow's lesson and prepared to leave. "Mathematics is essential, young lady! I don't want you turning out like those silly society women. Stick with it and you'll come to enjoy it." He patted her cheek. "It'll drive all the foolishness out of your head."
She turned to go, but he stopped her with a gesture and took an uncut book from the high desk.
"Here's some sort of Key to the Mysteries that your Heloise sent you. Religion! I don't interfere with anyone's beliefs... I've had a look at it. Take it. Well—go on, go."
He patted her on the shoulder and personally closed the door behind her.

Princess Mary returned to her room wearing the sad, anxious expression that rarely left her face and that made her plain, sickly features seem even plainer. She sat down at her writing desk, which was surrounded by miniature portraits and cluttered with books and papers. The princess was as messy as her father was orderly. She set down the geometry book and eagerly broke the seal on her letter. It was from her closest childhood friend—the very same Julie Karagina who had been at the Rostovs' name-day party.
Julie wrote in French:

Dear and precious Friend, How terrible and frightening it is to be separated! Though I tell myself that half my life and half my happiness are wrapped up in you, and that despite the distance between us our hearts are joined by unbreakable bonds, my heart rebels against fate, and despite all the pleasures and distractions around me, I cannot shake a certain secret sorrow that has lived in my heart ever since we parted. Why can't we be together as we were last summer, in your big study, on the blue sofa—the sofa where we shared our secrets? Why can't I draw fresh moral strength from your gaze, as I did three months ago—that gaze so gentle, calm, and searching, which I loved so much and seem to see before me now as I write?

Having read this far, Princess Mary sighed and glanced at the mirror on her right. It reflected a thin, graceless figure and a gaunt face. Her eyes, always sad, now looked with particular hopelessness at her own reflection. "She flatters me," the princess thought, looking away and continuing to read. But Julie was not flattering her friend. The princess's eyes—large, deep, and luminous, as though warm shafts of light sometimes radiated from them—were so beautiful that despite the plainness of her face, they often lent her a magnetism more powerful than conventional beauty. But the princess never saw the beautiful expression of her own eyes—the look they had when she wasn't thinking about herself. Like everyone, her face took on a forced, unnatural expression as soon as she looked in a mirror. She continued reading:

All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad; the other is with the Guards, who are about to march for the frontier. Our dear Emperor has left Petersburg, and it's believed he intends to expose his precious person to the dangers of war. God grant that the Corsican monster who is destroying the peace of Europe may be overthrown by the angel whom the Almighty, in His goodness, has given us as our sovereign! To say nothing of my brothers, this war has robbed me of one of the bonds dearest to my heart. I mean young Nicholas Rostov, who was so passionately enthusiastic that he couldn't bear to remain idle and has left the university to join the army. I will confess to you, dear Mary, that despite his extreme youth, his departure for the army was a great sorrow for me. This young man, of whom I told you last summer, is so noble-spirited and full of that genuine youthfulness one so rarely finds anymore among our old men of twenty—and above all, he is so honest and has so much heart. He is so pure and poetic that my relationship with him, brief as it was, has been one of the sweetest comforts to my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. Someday I'll tell you about our parting and everything that was said. It's all still too fresh. Ah, dear friend, you're lucky not to know these sharp joys and sorrows. You are fortunate, because the sorrows are usually stronger! I know perfectly well that Count Nicholas is too young ever to be more than a friend to me, but this sweet friendship, this poetic, pure bond, was exactly what my heart needed. But enough of this! The main news, the talk of all Moscow, is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Can you imagine! The three princesses received almost nothing, Prince Vasili got nothing at all, and it's Monsieur Pierre who has inherited everything and has been officially recognized as legitimate—so he is now Count Bezukhov and the owner of the greatest fortune in Russia. People say Prince Vasili played a thoroughly contemptible role in the whole affair and went back to Petersburg completely humiliated.

I'll admit I don't understand much about wills and inheritance, but I do know that ever since this young man—whom we all used to know as plain Monsieur Pierre—became Count Bezukhov and owner of one of the largest fortunes in Russia, I've been greatly entertained watching how the tone and manners of mothers with marriageable daughters, and of the young ladies themselves, have changed toward him. Though, between you and me, he always struck me as a rather unremarkable fellow. Since for the past two years people have amused themselves finding husbands for me—most of whom I don't even know—the Moscow matchmaking rumor mill now speaks of me as the future Countess Bezukhova. But you'll understand I have no interest in that title. Speaking of marriages: did you know that a while ago that universal busybody Anna Mikhaylovna told me, in the strictest confidence, about a marriage plan for you? It involves none other than Prince Vasili's son Anatole, whom they hope to reform through marriage to someone wealthy and distinguished—and you are the one his family has chosen. I don't know how you'll feel about it, but I thought it my duty to tell you. He's said to be very handsome and an absolute rogue. That's all I've been able to find out about him.

But enough gossip. I'm at the bottom of my second sheet of paper, and Mama has sent for me to go dine at the Apraksins'. Read the mystical book I'm sending you—it's an enormous success here. Though there are things in it that are hard for our feeble human minds to grasp, it is a wonderful book that calms and elevates the soul. Farewell! Give my respects to your father and my regards to Mademoiselle Bourienne. I embrace you as I love you.
JULIE
P.S. Send me news of your brother and his charming little wife.

The princess sat thinking for a while, a thoughtful smile on her face, her luminous eyes lighting up until her expression was completely transformed. Then she rose abruptly and, with her heavy step, went to the writing table. She took out a sheet of paper and her hand flew rapidly across it. This was her reply, also in French:

Dear and precious Friend, Your letter of the 13th brought me great joy. So you still love me, my romantic Julie? The separation you complain about so bitterly seems not to have had its usual effect on you. You speak of your loneliness—but what should I say, I who am cut off from everyone dear to me? Ah, if we didn't have religion to comfort us, life would be so bleak. Why do you think I would judge your feelings for that young man harshly? In such matters I am strict only with myself. I understand such feelings in others, and though I've never experienced them, I can neither approve nor condemn them. It only seems to me that Christian love—love of neighbor, love of one's enemy—is worthier, sweeter, and more beautiful than the feelings that a handsome young man's eyes can awaken in a romantic and loving young girl like you.

The news of Count Bezukhov's death reached us before your letter, and my father was deeply affected. He says the count was the last representative but one of the great century, and that his own turn is next—though he'll do everything he can to postpone it as long as possible. God spare us from that terrible misfortune!

I can't agree with you about Pierre, whom I've known since he was a child. He always seemed to me to have an excellent heart, and that is the quality I value most in people. As for his inheritance and Prince Vasili's role in it—how sad for both of them. Ah, my dear friend, how terribly true are our divine Savior's words: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of God. I pity Prince Vasili, but I feel even sorrier for Pierre. So young, and weighed down with such wealth—what temptations lie ahead of him! If anyone asked me what I desire most on earth, it would be to be poorer than the poorest beggar. A thousand thanks, dear friend, for the book you've sent, which is enjoying such success in Moscow. But since you tell me it contains things our weak minds cannot understand alongside its good things, it seems rather pointless to spend time on what is incomprehensible and therefore fruitless. I have never understood why some people enjoy confusing their minds with mystical books that only awaken doubt and inflame the imagination, giving them a tendency toward exaggeration entirely contrary to Christian simplicity. Let us read the Epistles and the Gospels instead. Let us not try to penetrate their mysteries, for how can we—wretched sinners that we are—presume to understand the terrible, holy secrets of Providence while we remain in this flesh, which is an impenetrable veil between us and the Eternal? Let us confine ourselves to the sublime rules our divine Savior left for our guidance here on earth. Let us try to follow them, and let us trust that the less we allow our feeble human minds to wander, the more we shall please God, who rejects all knowledge not from Him; and the less we try to fathom what He has chosen to conceal from us, the sooner He will reveal it through His divine Spirit.

My father has not spoken to me of a suitor, but has only mentioned that he received a letter and is expecting a visit from Prince Vasili. Regarding this marriage proposal, I will tell you, dear sweet friend, that I consider marriage a divine institution to which we must submit. However painful it may be, should the Almighty place upon me the duties of wife and mother, I will try to fulfill them as faithfully as I can, without troubling myself to examine my feelings toward whomever He may give me as a husband.

I've had a letter from my brother announcing his imminent arrival at Bald Hills with his wife. This pleasure will be short-lived, however, as he will be leaving again to take part in this terrible war into which we have been drawn—God knows how or why. Not only where you are, at the heart of affairs and society, but even here, amid farmwork and the tranquility of nature that city people think defines the countryside—here too the rumors of war are heard and felt painfully. My father talks of nothing but marches and countermarches, things I understand nothing about. And the day before yesterday, during my daily walk through the village, I witnessed a heartbreaking scene.... It was a column of conscripts drafted from our people, setting off to join the army. You should have seen the state of the mothers, wives, and children of the men who were leaving. You should have heard the weeping. It seems as if humanity has forgotten the laws of our divine Savior, who preached love and the forgiveness of wrongs—and that people now believe the highest merit lies in the skill of killing one another.
Farewell, dear and kind friend. May our divine Savior and His most Holy Mother keep you in Their holy and all-powerful care!
MARY

"Ah, so you're sending a letter, Princess? I've already sent mine. I wrote to my poor mother," said Mademoiselle Bourienne with a smile, speaking quickly in her pleasant, melodious voice with its rolling r's. She brought into Princess Mary's earnest, sorrowful world a completely different atmosphere—carefree, lighthearted, and self-satisfied.

"Princess, I should warn you," she added, lowering her voice and clearly enjoying the sound of it, speaking with exaggerated affectation, "the prince has been scolding Mikhail Ivanovich. He's in a terrible mood—very grim. Be prepared."
"Ah, dear friend," Princess Mary replied, "I've asked you never to tell me what mood my father is in. I don't allow myself to judge him, and I wouldn't want others to either."

The princess glanced at her watch and, seeing that she was five minutes late starting her practice on the clavichord, hurried into the sitting room with an anxious expression. Between twelve and two o'clock, according to the day's fixed schedule, the prince rested and the princess played the clavichord.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: The gray-haired valet sat drowsily listening to the prince snoring in his large study. From the far side of the house, through closed doors, came the sound of a difficult passage from a Dussek sonata—repeated twenty times over.

Just then, a closed carriage and a hooded cart pulled up to the front porch. Prince Andrew stepped out, helped his small wife down, and let her enter the house ahead of him. Old Tikhon, wearing a wig, poked his head out of the antechamber door, whispered that the prince was sleeping, and quickly shut it again. Tikhon knew that neither the son's arrival nor any other unusual event was allowed to disturb the appointed order of the day. Prince Andrew apparently knew this just as well as Tikhon. He checked his watch, as if to confirm whether his father's habits had changed since his last visit, and, satisfied that they hadn't, turned to his wife.
"He won't be up for twenty minutes. Let's go see Mary," he said.
The little princess had put on weight since they'd last been here, but her eyes and her short, downy upper lip—which lifted when she began to speak—were as merry and charming as ever.

"Why, this is a palace!" she said to her husband, looking around with the expression people use when complimenting their host at a ball. "Come on, quick, quick!" And she flashed a smile at Tikhon, at her husband, and at the footman escorting them.
"Is that Mary practicing? Let's sneak up and surprise her."
Prince Andrew followed her with a courteous but melancholy expression.
"You've gotten older, Tikhon," he said in passing to the old man, who kissed his hand.
Before they reached the room from which the clavichord music was coming, the pretty, fair-haired Frenchwoman, Mademoiselle Bourienne, burst out, apparently beside herself with excitement.
"Oh, what joy for the princess!" she cried. "At last! I must go tell her!"
"No, no, please don't... You're Mademoiselle Bourienne," said the little princess, kissing her. "I feel like I already know you through my sister-in-law's friendship. She wasn't expecting us?"
They approached the sitting room door, from which the same passage of the sonata could be heard repeating. Prince Andrew stopped and made a pained face, as if bracing for something unpleasant.

The little princess walked in. The music broke off mid-phrase, a cry rang out, followed by Princess Mary's heavy footsteps and the sound of kissing. When Prince Andrew entered, the two princesses—who had met only once before, briefly, at his wedding—were locked in each other's arms, pressing their lips to whatever part of each other's face they could reach. Mademoiselle Bourienne stood nearby with her hand pressed to her heart, wearing a blissful smile and looking equally prepared to burst into tears or laughter. Prince Andrew shrugged and frowned, the way music lovers do when they hear a wrong note. The two women released each other, then immediately seized each other's hands again, kissing them, pulling them away, and kissing each other's faces once more. To Prince Andrew's bewilderment, they both began to cry, then kissed again. Mademoiselle Bourienne started crying too. Prince Andrew was clearly uncomfortable, but to the two women it all felt perfectly natural—it apparently never crossed their minds that their meeting could have gone any other way.

"Oh, my dear!... Oh, Mary!..." they exclaimed simultaneously, then laughed. "I dreamed about you last night..." "You weren't expecting us?..." "Oh, Mary, you've gotten thinner!..." "And you've gotten heavier!..."
"I recognized the princess right away," Mademoiselle Bourienne put in.
"And I had no idea!..." Princess Mary exclaimed. "Oh, Andrew—I didn't even see you."

Prince Andrew and his sister took each other's hands and kissed, and he told her she was still the same crybaby she had always been. Princess Mary turned toward her brother, and through her tears the warm, loving, gentle light of her large, luminous eyes—extraordinarily beautiful in that moment—rested on Prince Andrew's face.

The little princess chattered nonstop. Her short, downy upper lip kept dipping to meet her rosy lower lip, then lifting again as her face broke into a smile of gleaming teeth and sparkling eyes. She told them about an accident they'd had on Spassky Hill that could have been serious in her condition, then immediately reported that she'd left all her clothes in Petersburg and heaven knew what she would wear here, and that Andrew had completely changed, and that Kitty Odyntsova had married an old man, and that there was a real suitor for Mary—but they'd discuss that later. Princess Mary watched her brother in silence, her beautiful eyes full of love and sadness. She was clearly following her own train of thought, independent of her sister-in-law's stream of words. In the middle of a description of the latest Petersburg party, she turned to her brother:
"So you're really going to the war, Andrew?" she asked with a sigh.
Lise sighed too.
"Yes—tomorrow, in fact," her brother replied.
"He's leaving me here, God knows why, when he could have had a promotion..."
Princess Mary didn't hear the rest. Following her own thoughts, she turned to her sister-in-law with a tender glance at her figure.
"Is it definite?" she asked.
The little princess's face changed. She sighed and said: "Yes, quite definite. Oh, it's so frightening..."
Her lip dropped. She brought her face close to her sister-in-law's and suddenly began to cry again.
"She needs to rest," Prince Andrew said with a frown. "Don't you, Lise? Take her to your room, and I'll go see Father. How is he? The same as ever?"
"Yes, exactly the same. Though I don't know what you'll make of it," the princess answered cheerfully.

"Same hours? Same walks along the avenues? And the lathe?" Prince Andrew asked with a barely perceptible smile, showing that despite all his love and respect for his father, he was well aware of his quirks.
"The same hours, and the lathe, and the mathematics, and my geometry lessons," Princess Mary said happily, as though geometry were among the greatest pleasures of her life.

When the twenty minutes were up and it was time for the old prince to rise, Tikhon came to summon the young prince. In honor of his son's arrival, the old man made an exception to his routine: he gave orders for Prince Andrew to be admitted to his rooms while he dressed for dinner. The old prince always dressed in the old-fashioned way—an antique-style coat and powdered hair. When Prince Andrew entered his father's dressing room—not wearing the contemptuous expression he put on in drawing rooms, but the lively face he showed when talking with Pierre—the old man was sitting in a large leather armchair, wrapped in a powdering cape, offering his head to Tikhon's ministrations.
"Ah, the warrior! Come to conquer Bonaparte?" the old man said, shaking his powdered head as much as the braid Tikhon was plaiting would allow.
"You'd better deal with him properly, or he'll have us all as his subjects before long! How are you?" And he offered his cheek.

The old man was in high spirits after his pre-dinner nap. (He used to say that a nap after dinner was silver, but before dinner was gold.) He cast fond, sidelong glances at his son from beneath those thick, bushy brows. Prince Andrew went over and kissed his father on the indicated spot. He made no comment on his father's favorite hobby—ridiculing modern-day military leaders, and Bonaparte in particular.
"Yes, Father, I've come with my wife, who is expecting," Prince Andrew said, watching his father's face with eager, respectful attention. "How is your health?"
"Only fools and wastrels get sick, my boy. You know me: I'm busy from morning to night, I'm moderate in everything—naturally I'm well."
"Thank God," said his son, smiling.

"God has nothing to do with it! Now then," he continued, returning to his favorite topic, "tell me how the Germans have been teaching you to fight Bonaparte with this new science of theirs—'strategy,' they call it."
Prince Andrew smiled.
"Give me a chance to catch my breath, Father," he said with a grin that showed his father's eccentricities didn't diminish his love or respect. "I haven't even had time to settle in!"

"Nonsense, nonsense!" the old man cried, tugging at his pigtail to test the braid, and grabbing his son's hand. "The house for your wife is ready. Princess Mary will take her over and show her around—they'll chatter to their hearts' content. That's how women are! I'm glad to have her. Sit down and talk. I understand about Mikhelson's army—and Tolstoy's too... a coordinated offensive... But what's the southern army supposed to do? Prussia is neutral—I know that. And Austria?" he said, rising from his chair and pacing the room while Tikhon trotted behind him, handing over various articles of clothing. "What about Sweden? How will they cross Pomerania?"

Prince Andrew, seeing his father wouldn't let it go, began reluctantly—but gradually with more and more animation, switching unconsciously from Russian to French as was his habit—to explain the campaign plan. He described how an army of ninety thousand was to threaten Prussia to force her out of neutrality and into the war; how part of that force would link up with Swedish troops at Stralsund; how two hundred and twenty thousand Austrians and a hundred thousand Russians would operate in Italy and on the Rhine; how fifty thousand Russians and an equal number of British would land at Naples; and how a combined force of five hundred thousand men was to attack the French from multiple directions. The old prince showed not the slightest interest during this explanation, continuing to dress and walk about as if he weren't listening. Three times he interrupted unexpectedly. Once he stopped the narrative by shouting: "The white one, the white one!"
This meant Tikhon was handing him the wrong waistcoat. Another time he broke in to say:
"And when is she due?" Then, shaking his head disapprovingly: "That's bad! Go on, go on."

The third interruption came as Prince Andrew was wrapping up. The old man began singing in the cracked voice of old age: "Malbrook s'en va-t-en guerre. Dieu sait quand reviendra." — Marlborough is off to war. God knows when he'll return.
* "Marlborough is going to the wars; God knows when he'll return."
His son only smiled.
"I'm not saying I approve of the plan," the son said. "I'm just telling you what it is. Napoleon has surely drawn up his own plan by now—and it's probably no worse than this one."
"Well, you haven't told me anything new," the old man said, and repeated meditatively, with quick rhythm:
"Dieu sait quand reviendra — God knows when he'll return. Now go to the dining room."

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 27
paragraphs: At the appointed hour, the prince—powdered and freshly shaved—entered the dining room, where his daughter-in-law, Princess Mary, and Mademoiselle Bourienne were already waiting, along with his architect. By one of the old prince's strange whims, this architect was admitted to the dinner table, even though his rank was far too modest to warrant such an honor. The prince, who was generally strict about social distinctions and seldom invited even important government officials to dine, had unexpectedly chosen Mikhail Ivanovich—a man who always retreated to a corner to blow his nose into a checkered handkerchief—to illustrate his theory that all men are equal. He had impressed upon his daughter more than once that Mikhail Ivanovich was "not one bit worse than you or me." At dinner, the prince usually directed more of his conversation at the silent Mikhail Ivanovich than at anyone else.

In the dining room—which, like every room in the house, had extraordinarily high ceilings—the household members and the footmen (one stationed behind each chair) stood waiting for the prince to appear. The head butler, napkin draped over his arm, was inspecting the table settings, signaling to the footmen, and glancing nervously between the clock and the door through which the prince would enter. Prince Andrew was studying a large gilt frame, new to him, that held the Bolkonski family tree. Opposite it hung a matching frame with a poorly painted portrait—clearly the work of a local artist—of a prince in a crown, supposedly a descendant of Rurik and ancestor of the Bolkonskys. Prince Andrew looked again at the family tree, shook his head, and laughed the way one laughs at a portrait so perfectly capturing its subject that it becomes comical.
"That's so completely him!" he said to Princess Mary, who had come up beside him.
Princess Mary looked at her brother in surprise. She didn't understand what he found funny. Everything their father did filled her with reverence and was beyond questioning.
"Everyone has their weak spot," Prince Andrew continued. "Imagine—with his formidable intellect, indulging in this kind of vanity!"

Princess Mary couldn't fathom the audacity of her brother's criticism and was about to respond when the expected footsteps were heard coming from the study. The prince walked in briskly and jauntily, as was his way, as though deliberately setting the liveliness of his manner against the rigid formality of his household. At that instant, the great clock struck two and was joined by a smaller clock chiming from the drawing room. The prince stopped. His sharp, glittering eyes swept sternly over everyone present and came to rest on the little princess. She felt what courtiers feel when the Tsar enters—a rush of fear and deference that the old man inspired in everyone around him. He stroked her hair and then gave her an awkward pat on the back of her neck.
"I'm glad—glad to see you," he said, looking attentively into her eyes, then walked quickly to his place and sat down. "Sit down, sit down! Sit down, Mikhail Ivanovich!"
He indicated a seat beside him for his daughter-in-law. A footman pulled out the chair for her.
"Well, well!" the old man said, eyeing her rounded figure. "You've been in quite a hurry. Not good!"
He laughed in his usual dry, cold, unpleasant way—with his lips only, not his eyes.
"You need to walk—walk as much as possible, as much as possible," he said.

The little princess either didn't hear his words or chose not to. She sat silent and seemed ill at ease. The prince asked about her father, and she began to smile and talk. He asked about mutual acquaintances, and she grew more animated, chattering away, passing on greetings from various people and retelling the latest society gossip.
"Countess Apraksina, the poor thing, lost her husband—she's cried her eyes out," she said, growing more and more lively.

As she became more animated, the prince studied her with increasing severity, and then suddenly, as if he had observed her long enough and formed a definite opinion, he turned away and addressed Mikhail Ivanovich.

"Well, Mikhail Ivanovich, things aren't looking good for our friend Bonaparte. Prince Andrew"—he always referred to his son this way—"has been telling me what forces are being gathered against him! And you and I never did think much of him."

Mikhail Ivanovich had no idea when "you and I" had ever said any such thing about Bonaparte, but understanding that he was being used as a convenient prop for the prince's favorite subject, he looked inquiringly at the young prince, wondering what would come next.
"He's a great tactician!" the prince said to his son, nodding toward the architect.

The conversation turned again to the war, to Bonaparte, and to the generals and statesmen of the day. The old prince seemed convinced not only that every man of the current age was an infant who didn't know the ABCs of warfare or politics, and that Bonaparte was an insignificant little Frenchman who had succeeded only because there were no Potemkins or Suvorovs left to oppose him—but also that there were no real political difficulties in Europe and no real war, only a sort of puppet show in which the men of the day were playing at something serious. Prince Andrew cheerfully endured his father's mockery of modern leaders, drawing him out and listening with obvious enjoyment.
"The past always seems better," he said. "But didn't Suvorov himself walk into a trap set by Moreau, from which he couldn't escape?"

"Who told you that? Who?" the prince cried. "Suvorov!" He shoved his plate away—Tikhon caught it deftly. "Suvorov!... Think, Prince Andrew. Two great commanders—Frederick and Suvorov. Moreau!... Moreau would have been taken prisoner if Suvorov had been given a free hand. But he had the Austrian war council—the Hofskriegsratschnapswurst—on his back. The devil himself couldn't have managed them! When you get out there, you'll see what those councils are really like! Suvorov couldn't handle them—so what chance does Mikhail Kutuzov have? No, my boy," he continued, "you and your generals won't be a match for Bonaparte. You'll have to bring in the French so that birds of a feather can fight together. They've sent the German Pahlen to New York to fetch the Frenchman Moreau," he said, referring to the invitation extended that year for Moreau to enter Russian service. "Wonderful!... Were the Potemkins, Suvorovs, and Orlovs Germans? No, my boy—either you've all lost your minds, or I've outlived mine. God help you, and we'll see what happens. They've made Bonaparte into a great commander among them! Ha!..."
"I'm not saying all the plans are good," Prince Andrew said. "I'm just surprised by your opinion of Bonaparte. Laugh all you want, but Bonaparte is a great general all the same!"

"Mikhail Ivanovich!" the old prince called to the architect, who had been quietly focused on his roast and was hoping to be forgotten. "Didn't I tell you Bonaparte was a great tactician? And now he's saying the same thing."
"Absolutely, your excellency," the architect replied.
The prince let out another of his cold laughs.

"Bonaparte was born lucky. He's got excellent soldiers. And besides, he started out by fighting Germans. Anyone who isn't a complete fool has been able to beat the Germans. Since the beginning of history, everyone has beaten the Germans. They've never beaten anyone—except each other. He made his reputation fighting them."

And the prince launched into a detailed account of all the blunders that, in his view, Bonaparte had made in his campaigns and even in politics. His son offered no rebuttal, but it was clear that no argument would change his mind any more than it would change his father's. He listened, held back his responses, and couldn't help marveling at how this old man, living alone in the country for so many years, could be so well-informed and so incisive about every recent military and political development in Europe.

"You think I'm just an old man who doesn't understand the world today?" his father concluded. "But it keeps me up at night. Well, tell me—where has this great commander of yours actually shown his genius?"
"That would take too long to explain," the son replied.
"Fine then, go worship your Bonaparte! Mademoiselle Bourienne, here's another admirer of that gunpowder-monkey emperor of yours," he said in excellent French.
"You know, Prince, I am not a Bonapartist!"
"Dieu sait quand reviendra" — God knows when he'll return — the prince hummed, out of tune, and with a laugh even more so, he left the table.

Throughout the entire discussion and the rest of dinner, the little princess had sat in silence, her frightened eyes darting between her father-in-law and Princess Mary. When they rose from the table, she took her sister-in-law by the arm and pulled her into another room.
"What a brilliant man your father is," she said. "Perhaps that's why I'm afraid of him."
"Oh, he is so kind!" Princess Mary answered.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 28
paragraphs: Prince Andrew was leaving the next evening. The old prince, never one to break his routine, had retired after dinner as usual. The little princess was in her sister-in-law's room. Prince Andrew, wearing a traveling coat without epaulettes, had been packing with his valet in the rooms set aside for him. After inspecting the carriage himself and watching the trunks being loaded, he ordered the horses harnessed. Only the things he always kept with him remained in his room: a small box, a large canteen fitted with silver tableware, two Turkish pistols, and a saber — a gift from his father, who had brought it back from the siege of Ochakov. All of Prince Andrew's traveling things were in perfect order: new, clean, and wrapped in cloth covers carefully tied with tape.

When setting out on a journey or changing their way of life, thoughtful people generally fall into a serious mood. At such moments a person reviews the past and plans for the future. Prince Andrew's face looked deeply thoughtful and tender. With his hands behind his back, he paced briskly from corner to corner of the room, staring straight ahead and shaking his head in thought. Was he afraid of going to war, or sad about leaving his wife? Perhaps both — but clearly he didn't want to be seen in that state, because when he heard footsteps in the corridor he quickly unclasped his hands, stopped by a table as though tying the cover of his small box, and put on his usual calm, impenetrable expression. It was the heavy tread of Princess Mary.

"I hear you've ordered the horses harnessed," she said breathlessly — she had obviously been running. "And I wanted so much to talk with you alone one more time! God knows how long we'll be apart. You're not angry that I came? You've changed so much, Andrusha," she added, as if to explain her question.

She smiled as she used his pet name, "Andrusha." It was clearly strange for her to think that this stern, handsome man was the same Andrusha — the skinny, mischievous boy she had played with as a child.
"And where is Lise?" he asked, answering her question with nothing more than a smile.

"She was so tired she fell asleep on the sofa in my room. Oh, Andrew! What a treasure of a wife you have," she said, sitting down on the sofa facing her brother. "She's practically a child — such a dear, cheerful child. I've grown so fond of her."
Prince Andrew said nothing, but the princess caught the look of irony and contempt that crossed his face.

"We should be patient with small weaknesses — who doesn't have them, Andrew? Don't forget she was raised in high society, so her position now is hardly an easy one. We should try to understand everyone's situation. Tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner — to understand all is to forgive all. Think what it must be like for her, poor thing — after the life she was used to — to be separated from her husband and left alone in the country, and in her condition. It's very hard."
* Tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner.
Prince Andrew smiled at his sister the way we smile at people we think we understand completely.
"You live in the country and don't find it terrible," he replied.

"That's... different. Why talk about me? I don't want any other life, and couldn't have one, because I've never known anything else. But think, Andrew — a young society woman buried in the country during the best years of her life, all alone. Papa is always busy, and I... well, you know how little I have to offer in the way of entertainment to a woman used to the finest company. There's only Mademoiselle Bourienne..."
"I don't like your Mademoiselle Bourienne at all," said Prince Andrew.

"Really? She's very kind and nice, and above all, she deserves pity. She has no one — no one at all. To tell the truth, I don't really need her, and she's even a bit in my way. You know I've always been something of a loner, and I'm even more so now. I like being alone... Father likes her very much. She and Mikhail Ivanovich are the two people he's always gentle and kind to, because he's been a benefactor to both of them. As Sterne says: 'We don't love people so much for the good they've done us as for the good we've done them.' Father took her in when she was left homeless after her own father died. She's very good-natured, and Father likes the way she reads. She reads aloud to him in the evenings, and she does it beautifully."
"Let me be frank, Mary — I'd guess Father's personality makes things difficult for you sometimes, doesn't it?" Prince Andrew asked suddenly.
Princess Mary was first surprised, then horrified by the question.
"Difficult for me? For me?... Difficult for me!" she stammered.
"He was always rather harsh, and I'd imagine he's become quite trying now," said Prince Andrew, apparently speaking lightly about their father to test his sister.

"You are good in every way, Andrew, but you have a kind of intellectual pride," the princess said, following her own train of thought rather than the thread of the conversation, "and that's a great sin. How can anyone judge Father? And even if someone could, what feeling other than reverence could a man like our father inspire? I am so content and happy with him. I only wish all of you were as happy as I am."
Her brother shook his head, unconvinced.

"The only thing that's hard for me — I'll tell you the truth, Andrew — is Father's attitude toward religion. I can't understand how a man of his extraordinary intellect can fail to see what's as clear as day, and can go so far astray. That's the only thing that makes me unhappy. But even in this, I've noticed a slight improvement lately. His sarcasm about it has been less bitter recently, and he received a monk the other day and had a long conversation with him."
"Oh, my dear — I'm afraid you and your monk are wasting your ammunition," said Prince Andrew with a teasing but affectionate tone.
"Oh, my dear friend, I only pray and hope that God will hear me. Andrew..." she said timidly after a moment of silence, "I have a great favor to ask of you."
"What is it, dear?"

"No — promise you won't refuse! It won't cause you any trouble and it's nothing beneath you, but it would comfort me. Promise, Andrusha!" she said, reaching into her handbag but not yet taking out whatever she was holding, as if the object itself were the request and couldn't be shown until the promise was made.
She looked at her brother timidly.
"Even if it were a great deal of trouble..." Prince Andrew replied, seeming to guess what it was about.

"Think whatever you want! I know you're just like Father. Think what you like, but do this for my sake! Please! Father's father — our grandfather — wore it through all his wars." She still hadn't taken out what was in her handbag. "So you promise?"
"Of course. What is it?"
"Andrew, I want to bless you with this icon, and you must promise never to take it off. Do you promise?"

"As long as it doesn't weigh a hundred pounds and break my neck... To please you..." said Prince Andrew. But seeing immediately the pained expression his joke had brought to his sister's face, he caught himself and added: "I'm glad — really, dear, I'm very glad."

"Against your will He will save you and show you mercy and bring you to Himself, for in Him alone is truth and peace," she said in a voice trembling with emotion, solemnly holding up before her brother with both hands a small, oval, antique icon of the Savior with a dark face in a gold setting, on a finely wrought silver chain.
She crossed herself, kissed the icon, and handed it to Andrew.
"Please, Andrew, for my sake!"

Rays of gentle light shone from her large, timid eyes. Those eyes illuminated her whole thin, sickly face and made it beautiful. Her brother reached for the icon, but she stopped him. Andrew understood — he crossed himself and kissed it. His expression held tenderness, for he was genuinely moved, but also a glint of irony.
"Thank you, my dear." She kissed him on the forehead and sat back down on the sofa. They were silent for a moment.

"As I was saying, Andrew — be kind and generous, the way you always used to be. Don't judge Lise too harshly," she began again. "She's so sweet, so good-natured, and her situation right now is very hard."
"I don't recall complaining about my wife to you, Masha, or blaming her. Why are you saying all this?"
Red blotches appeared on Princess Mary's face, and she fell silent as though she felt guilty.
"I said nothing to you, but others have already spoken to you about it. And that makes me sorry," he continued.

The blotches deepened on her forehead, neck, and cheeks. She tried to speak but couldn't. Her brother had guessed correctly: the little princess had been crying after dinner, talking about her fears regarding her pregnancy and how much she dreaded it, complaining about her fate, her father-in-law, and her husband. After crying, she had fallen asleep. Prince Andrew felt sorry for his sister.

"Listen, Masha — I have nothing to reproach my wife with, and I never have, and I never will. And I have nothing to reproach myself with toward her either — and it will always be that way, no matter what circumstances I find myself in. But if you want the truth... if you want to know whether I'm happy? No. Is she happy? No. But why it's so — I don't know..."

As he said this he stood up, went to his sister, and bent down to kiss her forehead. His fine eyes lit up with a thoughtful, kind brightness that was rare for him, but he was looking not at his sister — he was gazing past her, over her head, into the darkness of the open doorway.

"Let's go to her — I need to say goodbye. Or else go wake her, and I'll come in a moment. Petrusha!" he called to his valet. "Come here, take these things. Put this on the seat and this on the right side."

Princess Mary got up and moved toward the door, then stopped and said: "Andrew, if you had faith, you would have turned to God and asked Him to give you the love you don't feel, and your prayer would have been answered."
"Well — maybe!" said Prince Andrew. "Go on, Masha. I'll come right away."

On the way to his sister's room, in the corridor connecting one wing of the house to the other, Prince Andrew ran into Mademoiselle Bourienne, who was smiling sweetly. It was the third time that day she had appeared before him with that ecstatic, seemingly artless smile in some secluded passageway.
"Oh! I thought you were in your room," she said, blushing for some reason and dropping her eyes.

Prince Andrew looked at her coldly, and an expression of anger suddenly crossed his face. He said nothing, but stared at her forehead and hair without meeting her eyes, with such contempt that the Frenchwoman blushed and slipped away without a word. When he reached his sister's room, his wife was already awake, and her cheerful voice, words tumbling out one after another, came through the open door. She was speaking in French, as always, and as if after a long period of self-restraint she was trying to make up for lost time.
"No, but imagine old Countess Zubova with those fake curls and her mouth full of false teeth, as if she were trying to cheat old age... Ha, ha, ha! Mary!"

Prince Andrew had already heard this exact sentence about Countess Zubova, and the same laugh, from his wife about five times in the company of others. He entered the room quietly. The little princess — plump and rosy — was sitting in an easy chair with her needlework in her hands, chattering away, repeating reminiscences and pet phrases from Petersburg. Prince Andrew came up, stroked her hair, and asked if she felt rested after the journey. She answered and went on talking.

A coach drawn by six horses stood waiting at the front steps. It was an autumn night, so dark the coachman couldn't see the carriage pole. Servants carrying lanterns bustled around the entrance. The enormous house blazed with light pouring through its tall windows. The household servants were crowded in the front hall, waiting to say goodbye to the young prince. Everyone was gathered in the reception room: Mikhail Ivanovich, Mademoiselle Bourienne, Princess Mary, and the little princess. Prince Andrew had been called to his father's study — the old man wanted to say goodbye in private. They were all waiting for the two of them to come out.
When Prince Andrew entered the study, the old man was sitting at his desk in the old-fashioned spectacles and white dressing gown he wore for no one but his son, writing. He glanced up.
"Leaving?" And he went back to his writing.
"I've come to say goodbye."
"Kiss me here." He pointed to his cheek. "Thank you. Thank you!"
"What are you thanking me for?"

"For not wasting time and not hanging on to a woman's apron strings. Duty comes first. Thank you, thank you!" And he went on writing, his pen sputtering and squeaking. "If you have something to say, say it. I can do two things at once," he added.
"About my wife... I feel bad enough as it is, leaving her in your care..."
"Stop talking nonsense. Say what you mean."
"When it's time for her to give birth, send to Moscow for a doctor. Have him come here."
The old prince stopped writing and stared at his son with stern eyes, as if he didn't understand.

"I know that if nature doesn't do its work, no one can help," said Prince Andrew, obviously uncomfortable. "I know that out of a million cases, only one goes badly. But it's what she wants, and what I want too. People have been telling her things. She had a dream and she's frightened."
"Hmm... hmm..." the old prince muttered to himself as he finished what he was writing. "I'll take care of it."
He signed with a flourish, then suddenly turned to his son and laughed.
"It's a bad situation, isn't it?"
"What's bad, Father?"
"The wife!" the old prince said, brief and pointed.
"I don't understand!" said Prince Andrew.
"There's nothing to be done about it, son," the prince said. "They're all the same — you can't un-marry. Don't worry, I won't tell anyone. But you know it yourself."
He seized his son's hand with his small, bony fingers, shook it, stared straight into his face with sharp eyes that seemed to see right through him, and laughed again — that cold laugh of his.

The son sighed, silently admitting that his father had understood him. The old man went on folding and sealing his letter, snatching up the wax, the seal, and the paper and tossing them aside with his usual rapid movements.
"What can you do? She's pretty! I'll take care of everything. Set your mind at ease," he said in short, clipped phrases as he sealed the letter.
Andrew said nothing; he was both glad and uneasy that his father understood him. The old man stood and handed the letter to his son.

"Listen," he said. "Don't worry about your wife — what can be done will be done. Now listen: give this letter to Mikhail Ilarionovich. I've written that he should put you to good use in real assignments and not keep you stuck as an adjutant — it's a dead-end position. Tell him I remember him and think well of him. And write to tell me how he receives you. If he treats you well, serve him. A son of Nicholas Bolkonski doesn't need to serve under anyone who's out of favor. Now come here."
(Kutuzov.)

He spoke so fast he didn't finish half his words, but his son was used to understanding him. He led Andrew to the desk, raised the lid, pulled open a drawer, and took out an exercise book filled with his bold, tall, dense handwriting.

"I'll probably die before you do. So remember — these are my memoirs. Give them to the Emperor after I'm gone. Now here's a government bond and a letter — it's a prize for whoever writes a history of Suvorov's campaigns. Send it to the Academy. And here are some notes for you to read after I'm dead. You'll find them useful."
Andrew did not tell his father he would surely live many more years. He felt he shouldn't say it.
"I'll do it all, Father," he said.

"Very well. Now — goodbye!" He held out his hand for his son to kiss, then embraced him. "Remember this, Prince Andrew: if they kill you, it will grieve me — your old father..." He paused abruptly, then in a shrill, cracking voice suddenly cried out: "But if I learn that you did not conduct yourself as a son of Nicholas Bolkonski, I will be ashamed!"
"You didn't need to say that, Father," the son replied with a smile.
The old man was silent.
"I also wanted to ask you," Prince Andrew continued, "if I'm killed and if I have a son — don't let him be taken away from you, as I mentioned yesterday. Let him grow up with you... Please."
"Not let the wife have him?" said the old man, and laughed.
They stood facing each other in silence. The old man's sharp eyes were fixed on his son's. Something twitched in the lower part of the old prince's face.
"We've said goodbye. Go!" he shouted suddenly in a loud, angry voice, and flung the door open.

"What is it? What's wrong?" both princesses exclaimed when they caught a momentary glimpse at the doorway of Prince Andrew and the old man behind him — white dressing gown, spectacles, no wig — shouting in an angry voice.
Prince Andrew sighed and said nothing.
"Well!" he said, turning to his wife.
And the way he said "Well!" was coldly ironic, as if to say: Now go ahead with your performance.
"Andrew — already!" said the little princess, turning pale and looking at her husband with alarm.
He embraced her. She cried out and fainted against his shoulder.
He carefully freed the shoulder she was leaning on, looked into her face, and gently settled her into an armchair.
"Goodbye, Mary," he said softly to his sister, taking her hand and kissing it, and then he walked out of the room with quick steps.

The little princess lay in the armchair while Mademoiselle Bourienne rubbed her temples. Princess Mary, still holding her sister-in-law's arm, gazed with her beautiful, tear-filled eyes at the door through which Prince Andrew had gone and made the sign of the cross in his direction. From the study, like pistol shots, came the repeated sound of the old man furiously blowing his nose. The moment Prince Andrew left, the study door flew open and the stern figure of the old man in his white dressing gown appeared.
"Gone? Good!" he said. And glancing angrily at the unconscious little princess, he shook his head in disapproval and slammed the door.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: In October 1805, a Russian army was occupying the villages and towns of the Archduchy of Austria, while fresh regiments still arriving from Russia were settling around the fortress of Braunau and burdening the local residents on whom they were billeted. Braunau served as the headquarters of the commander in chief, Kutuzov.

On October 11, 1805, one of the infantry regiments that had just reached Braunau was halted half a mile from town, waiting to be inspected by the commander in chief. Despite the distinctly un-Russian landscape — fruit orchards, stone fences, tiled roofs, and hills in the distance — and despite the fact that the curious locals staring at the soldiers were not Russian, the regiment looked exactly like any Russian regiment preparing for inspection anywhere in the heart of Russia.

The evening before, an order had come down that the commander in chief would inspect the regiment while on the march. Although the wording was unclear to the regimental commander — there was some question about whether the troops should be in marching order or not — a conference of battalion commanders decided to present the regiment in full parade formation, on the principle that it's always better to bow too low than not low enough. So after a twenty-mile march, the soldiers were kept up all night mending and polishing without a moment's sleep, while adjutants and company commanders calculated and recounted, and by morning the regiment — instead of the straggling, disorderly mob it had been on its march the day before — presented a well-ordered display of two thousand men, each of whom knew his place and his duty, with every button and every strap in position, shining with cleanliness. And not only was the exterior in order; had the commander in chief cared to look beneath the uniforms, he would have found a clean shirt on every man and in every knapsack the regulation number of articles — "needle, soap, and all," as the soldiers liked to say. There was only one problem no one could solve: the state of the men's boots. More than half were full of holes. But this wasn't the regimental commander's fault — he had submitted repeated requests, and the Austrian commissariat had simply never delivered the boots. The regiment had marched some seven hundred miles.

The regimental commander was an elderly, hot-tempered, heavyset general with grizzled eyebrows and whiskers, broader from chest to back than across the shoulders. He wore a brand-new uniform still showing its fold creases and thick gold epaulettes that seemed to stand up rather than lie flat on his massive shoulders. He had the air of a man happily performing one of the most solemn duties of his life. He walked back and forth in front of the ranks, pulling himself up and slightly arching his back at every step. It was clear the commander adored his regiment, took immense pride in it, and thought of nothing else — yet his strutting walk also suggested that military matters were not the only thing on his mind, and that social life and the fair sex occupied no small corner of his thoughts.

"Well, Mikhail Mitrich, sir?" he said, addressing one of the battalion commanders, who pressed forward with a smile. It was obvious they were both in high spirits. "We had our hands full last night. Still, I'd say the regiment doesn't look half bad, eh?"
